source_text: Vir profecto heroicis connumerandus ingeniis, claritudine rerum et coalita maiestate conspicuus.
excerpt_note: The first sentence of 25.4, the opening of Ammianus' character sketch of Julian; the next sentence lists the four cardinal virtues. LacusCurtius has the same sentence on its book 25 page but does not name the edition of its Latin there.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: hērōicīs: from Greek hērōikos; long ē and ō, short i; not machine-checked.
maiestāte: the first syllable is long by position (mai-, consonantal i); some dictionaries mark māiestās; left unmarked here.
coalitā: short a and i (coalitus), long final ā of the ablative; not machine-checked.
clāritūdine: long ā and ū, as in clārus; not machine-checked.

translation: He was truly a man to be counted among the heroic natures, outstanding for the renown of his deeds and for a majesty that had grown to be part of him.
translation_note: The sentence has no main verb: supply est, "he is (to be counted)", with connumerandus, a gerundive. coalita maiestas is a dignity that has grown together with him, so ingrained rather than put on.

essay.t: Ammianus was born around 330 into a noble Greek family, probably at Antioch (the traditional view, which Britannica follows). He served in the army under the general Ursicinus, and later on Julian's Persian campaign.
At the end of his history he calls himself "once a soldier and a Greek", and says he wrote from the reign of Nerva to the death of Valens.
Only the last eighteen of his thirty-one books survive, covering 353 to 378; the work began where the Histories of Tacitus end.
Britannica calls him the last major Roman historian; that a Greek from Antioch chose to write in Latin is part of his interest, though why he did so he does not say in these passages.
Julian, born in 331 or 332, publicly announced his conversion to paganism in 361 and so was called the Apostate; he died on 26 or 27 June 363 during the Persian war.

In Ammianus' account the wounded emperor spent his last hours debating the sublimity of souls with the philosophers Maximus and Priscus, asked for cold water, and died in the middle of the night, in his thirty-second year.
The scene recalls the death of Socrates; that echo is my reading, not a claim Ammianus makes.

The obituary opens with this sentence and then grades Julian on the four cardinal virtues, temperance, prudence, justice and fortitude, and four external ones, military skill, authority, good fortune and generosity.

Yet Ammianus is not simply a fan: in the same sketch he calls harsh Julian's law barring Christian teachers of rhetoric and grammar unless they turned to the gods, and earlier he says it should be buried in eternal silence.

Britannica notes that, though both were pagans, Ammianus criticized Julian's religious policies while admiring him as a man, soldier and leader, and that many readers see Julian as the hero of the work.
How much of the portrait is admiration and how much is judgment remains a matter of reading.

questions.q: How does Ammianus describe himself at the end of his history?
options: Once a soldier and a Greek

questions.q: Which of Julian's measures does Ammianus criticize?
options: His lowering of the provincial taxes

All 31 books, from Nerva to Valens
Only the obituary of Julian in book 25
